     ​         Defendant Dasagroup Holdings Corp. hereby replies to the opposition filed by Plaintiff
 1
     Jefferies Funding, LLC in response to Dasagroup’s motion to dismiss the First Amended
 2
     Complaint (“FAC”):
 3
         I.​   PLAINTIFF HAS NOT MET ITS BURDEN TO SHOW THAT THE COURT HAS
 4             HAD SUBJECT MATTER JURISDICTION THROUGHOUT THIS LAWSUIT.
 5   ​         Jefferies’s opposition does not meaningfully respond to the considerable defects in
 6   justiciability caused by the intervening assignments of rights in tort and contract that had
 7   purportedly given it the standing to assert tort and contract claims arising out of the Silo Instant

 8   Pay Agreement. Rather than meet its burden in response to Dasagroup’s factual challenge to

 9   subject matter jurisdiction, it instead feigns disbelief and makes the baseless suggestion that any

10   challenge has been waived or is “foreclosed,” which is preposterous and contrary to binding

11   precedent from the U.S. Supreme Court. Jefferies also tries to hide behind Silo, arguing, without
     any authority, that while it maintained this lawsuit based on a purported assignment of rights
12
     from Silo and/or a right to collect under UCC 9-607 — i.e., Cal. Comm. Code § 9607 — it
13
     and/or Silo were apparently free to assign-away those rights to other entities to pursue other
14
     efforts against Dasagroup while this case was pending.
15
               A.​    Issues of Subject Matter Jurisdiction Can Never Be Forfeited or Waived.
16
               Contrary to what Plaintiffs argue (at Opp. pp. 13:13-21), there is no bar or waiver for
17
     challenge to subject matter jurisdiction. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(h)(3) (“If the court determines at
18
     any time that it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, the court must dismiss the action.”). “Subject
19
     matter jurisdiction can never be forfeited or waived and federal courts have a continuing
20
     independent obligation to determine whether subject-matter jurisdiction exists.” Leeson v.
21
     Transamerica Disability Income Plan, 671 F.3d 969, 975 n.12 (9th Cir. 2012) (internal quotation
22   marks and citations omitted). This is a clear, repeated directive from the Supreme Court. See,
23   e.g., United States v. Cotton, 535 U.S. 625, 630 (2002) (subject matter jurisdiction “can never be
24   forfeited or waived”); United States v. Hays, 515 U.S. 737, 742 (1995) (“The question of
25   standing is not subject to waiver . . .”). As one federal court has put it: “It is never too late in the
26   progression of an action for a motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Fed.
27   R. Civ. P. 12(h)(3) and Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(1).” Hu v. Skadden, 76 F.Supp.2d 476, 478

28   (S.D.N.Y. 1999).

                     REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS FIRST AM. COMPLAINT
                                                        2           Jefferies Funding v. Dasagroup Holdings et al.
                                                                    No. 3:24-cv-05639-TLT
          Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT          Document 143         Filed 09/10/25         Page 3 of 10


            B.​     Jefferies Has Failed to Meet Its Burden to Produce Affidavits or Other
 1
                    Evidence of Its Standing and Key Aspects of Subject Matter Jurisdiction.
 2          For unknown reasons, Jefferies’s opposition does not offer any evidence to substantiate
 3   its claim of subject matter jurisdiction over the original case that it filed, which is why the
 4   jurisdictional challenge should be granted. “On a motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter
 5   jurisdiction under Rule 12(b)(1), it is the plaintiff's burden to establish the existence of subject
 6   matter jurisdiction.” Center for Biological Diversity v. EPA, 316 F. Supp. 3d 1156, 1163
 7   (N.D.Cal. 2018) (quoting Kingman Reef Atoll Invs., LLC v. United States, 541 F.3d 1189, 1197

 8   (9th Cir. 2008)).

 9          A party challenging the court's subject matter jurisdiction under Rule 12(b)(1) may do so

10   via a facial challenge or a factual challenge. See White v. Lee, 227 F.3d 1214, 1242 (9th Cir.

11   2000). In evaluating a facial challenge to subject matter jurisdiction, the court accepts the factual
     allegations in the complaint as true. See Miranda v. Reno, 238 F.3d 1156, 1157 n.1 (9th Cir.
12
     2001). If, however, a defendant brings a factual challenge, then “a court may look beyond the
13
     complaint to matters of public record without having to convert the motion into one for summary
14
     judgment.” White, 227 F.3d at 1242 (citation omitted).
15
     ​      When, as here, a moving party has made a factual challenge to subject matter jurisdiction
16
     by offering affidavits or other evidence to dispute the allegations in the complaint — like, for
17
     instance, the Washington state UCC filings offered by Dasagroup that were filed after Jefferies
18
     filed this lawsuit — the party opposing the motion must “present affidavits or any other
19
     evidence necessary to satisfy its burden of establishing that the court, in fact, possesses subject
20
     matter jurisdiction.” Colwell v. Dep't of Health & Human Servs., 558 F.3d 1112, 1121 (9th Cir.
21   2009) (quoting St. Clair v. City of Chico, 880 F.2d 199, 201 (9th Cir. 1989)).
22          Here, Jefferies offers nothing but rote citations to the pleadings and feigned annoyance
23   and incredulity about the jurisdictional challenge. It offers nothing in the way of evidence other
24   than a reference to its prior pleadings. See Opp. at 13-14 (arguing, with no evidentiary support,
25   that “Jefferies has continuously maintained a justiciable interest in this lawsuit throughout its
26   pendency”). But arguments and statements of counsel are not evidence, and are not sufficient for

27   Jefferies to meet its burden to produce evidence to withstand a fact-based jurisdictional

28   challenge. See, e.g., Barcamerica Int’l USA Tr. v. Tyfield Importers, Inc., 289 F.3d 589, 593 n.4

     (9th Cir. 2002) (arguments of counsel are not evidence); Moran v. Selig, 447 F.3d 748, 759-60
 1
     (9th Cir. 2006) (unverified pleadings are not evidence).
 2
             C.​     By Its Own Admission, Jefferies Did Not Have Article III Standing To Sue on
 3                   Behalf of Silo for Harms to Silo When This Lawsuit Was First Filed.
 4           The Supreme Court has held that “when standing is questioned by a court or an opposing
 5   party, the litigant invoking the court’s jurisdiction must do more than simply allege a nonobvious
 6   harm. . . . [T]o cross the standing threshold, the litigant must explain how the elements essential
 7   to standing are met.” Va. House of Delegates v. Bethune-Hill, 587 U.S. 658, 663 (2019). To

 8   establish standing to sue, a plaintiff bears the burden of showing (1) an injury in fact, meaning an

 9   injury that is concrete and particularized, and actual or imminent; (2) a causal connection

10   between the injury and the causal conduct; and (3) a likelihood that the injury will be redressed

11   by a favorable decision. See Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 561 (1992).
     “Standing . . . is to be determined as of the commencement of suit,” Lujan, 504 U.S. at 570 n. 5,
12
     and a court may not permit an action to continue, even where the jurisdictional deficiencies have
13
     been subsequently cured if jurisdiction was lacking at commencement. See Cortlandt St.
14
     Recovery Corp. v. Hellas Telecomms, 790 F.3d 411, 422 (2d Cir. 2015); see also, Utah Ass'n of
15
     Ctys. v. Bush, 455 F.3d 1094, 1101 & n.6 (10th Cir. 2006) (“[b]ecause standing is determined as
16
     of the time of the filing of the complaint,” an alleged subsequent injury could not serve as a basis
17
     for plaintiff’s standing).
18
             By its rambling opposition, Jeffeires digs a bigger hole for itself that it cannot escape.
19
     Instead of producing evidence of the underlying chain of assignments, documentation, and/or
20
     security agreements that allegedly provided it with a legal basis to pursue Dasagroup when this
21   case was filed, Jefferies effectively concedes that it did not have standing to sue on behalf of Silo
22   and was exclusively suing on its purported rights as a secured party under UCC 9-607. See Opp.
23   at 7:15-17 (stating, inter alia, that “Jefferies initially held a security interest in the Affected
24   Receivables,” but only citing Compl. [Dkt 1] ¶¶ 1-3, 36-42 as proof of such interest).
25           Without more, none of those averments demonstrate that Jefferies had a right to bring a
26   direct action against Dasagroup on behalf of Silo for harms that were uniquely pleaded in the

27   original complaint as harms to Silo, not Jefferies. It is beyond dispute that a party lacking

28   privity of contract does not have standing to enforce an agreement and certainly has no basis to

     claim fraud or conversion with respect to other conduct related to such contract. See, e.g.,
 1
     Hatchwell v. Blue Shield of California, 198 Cal. App. 3d 1027, 1034 (1988). Perhaps
 2
     recognizing its error, Jefferies’s opposition attempts to hide behind the Forbearance Agreement,
 3
     suggesting that it was the original basis for its claims and has been a continual interest
 4
     maintained by Jefferies since the litigation began. See Opp. at 7:18-25. But that
 5
     mischaracterizes the original complaint, which speaks for itself.
 6
            The three claims Jefferies originally pleaded against Dasagroup when this case was filed
 7
     all arose from Dasagroup’s participation and course of performance toward Silo in connection
 8
     with the Instant Pay Program, not the Forbearance Agreement. These claims were pleaded
 9   separate and apart from any of Jefferies’s rights under the Forbearance Agreement, and the
10   conduct at issue pertained to events that occurred before Jefferies had announced its presence to
11   Dasagroup and before the later Forbearance Agreement between Jefferies and Dasagroup was
12   executed or allegedly breached. See Dkt. 1 (Original Complaint) at ¶¶ 47-57 (pleading Count I,
13   breach of contract, arising from Silo-Dasagroup Instant Pay contract, not the Jefferies-Dasagroup
14   Forbearance Agreement); ¶¶ 58-63 (pleading Count II, fraud, arising from representations made

15   by Dasagroup/Kickhass in “April and May of 2024 . . . that London Fruit had not made

16   payments on the Affected Receivables”); and ¶¶ 64-71 (pleading Count III, conversion, based

17   upon discovery that “[f]rom review of Kickhass’s bank statements,” Kickhass had received

18   considerable payments “from London Fruit in May 2024, . . . in June 2024[,] and . . . in July
     2024”). None of these allegations establish Jefferies’s standing to sue on behalf of Silo on the
19
     claims originally pleaded.
20
            Jefferies’s reliance on its purported status as a “secured party” under UCC 9-607 is also
21
     not convincing and does not establish its Article III standing with respect to the lawsuit it
22
     originally filed. Jefferies’s pleading is rather misleading because the “secured party” status it
23
     refers to is a status conferred by a different agreement — the “Silo Forbearance Agreement”
24
     — that Jeffereies entered into with Silo Capital, not Dasagroup. Section 9607(e) of the
25
     California Commercial Code is clear that the statute “does not determine whether an account
26
     debtor, bank, or other person obligated on collateral owes a duty to a secured party.” Cal.
27   Comm. Code§ 9607(e) (emphasis added). The commentary to section 9607 also states, with
28

                                                                  No. 3:24-cv-05639-TLT

     emphasis, that “[n]either this section nor former section 9-502 should be understood to regulate
 1
     the duties of an account debtor or other person obligated on collateral. Subsection (e) makes
 2
     this explicit.” Cal. Comm. Code § 9607, com 6.
 3
            Accordingly, UCC 9-607 does not impose any obligations upon, or provide any recourse
 4
     against, account debtors like Dasagroup; instead, it merely governs the rights and liabilities as to
 5
     collateral only existing between the secured party [i.e., Jefferies] and borrower [i.e., Silo/Silo
 6
     Capital] under any pertinent instrument [the “Silo Forbearance Agreement”]. See Dkt. 1 (Orig.
 7
     Complaint) ¶¶ 3, 11. The statute says nothing, and confers no Article III standing for Jefferies to
 8
     sue Dasagroup for injuries to parties like Silo. See Western Alliance Bank v. Nat'l Union Fire
 9   Ins. Co., 2016 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 19936, at *9, n.43 (N.D.Cal. Feb. 18, 2016) (holding that Cal.
10   Comm. Code § 9607 [i.e., UCC 9-607] “does not determine whether an account debtor . . . or
11   other person obligated on collateral owes a duty to a secured party”) (citing Cal. Com. Code §
12   9607(e) and BNY Midwest Trust Co. v. Nat'l Union Fire Ins. Co of Pittsburgh, 213 F. App'x 563,
13   567 (9th Cir. 2006)). In BNY Midwest Trust, the Ninth Circuit held a security interest in
14   “proceeds” of an instrument like a fidelity bond “does not confer standing to bring a claim for

15   losses suffered by parties other than the insured” on the bond. This is indistinguishable from

16   Jefferies’s suggestion that it had rights to sue Dasagroup on behalf of Silo under the opaque,

17   unsubstantiated, and un-produced “Silo Forbearance Agreement” that, it claims, gave it the right

18   to claim an interest in any amounts due from Dasagroup to Silo.
            The law is clear: “[I]n order to be able to sue in his or her own name, [an] assignee must
19
     obtain ownership of the claim, as opposed to merely a power of attorney regarding the claim.”
20
     Lasala v. Needham & Co., 2006 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 7388, at *23 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 24, 2006) (citing
21
     Advanced Magnetics, Inc. v. Bayfront Partners, Inc., 106 F.3d 11, 17 (2d Cir. 1997)) (emphasis in
22
     original). Nothing in the' original complaint states that Jefferies had received an assigned
23
     ownership interest in the claims it asserted in the original lawsuit it filed. And, as shown above,
24
     all of the claims it asserted were premised upon its standing to sue for harms to Silo with respect
25
     to the Instant Pay Program. It was not until later, before the FAC was filed, when Jefferies
26
     purports to have received a “assign[ment]” of the affected receivables “and all claims in any way
27   related to the Affected Receivables.” See, e.g., FAC ¶¶ 91, 102, 108.
28

                  REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS FIRST AM. COMPLAINT
                                                       6           Jefferies Funding v. Dasagroup Holdings et al.
                                                                   No. 3:24-cv-05639-TLT
        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT            Document 143         Filed 09/10/25          Page 7 of 10


            Jefferies’s failure to substantiate its standing to have filed the lawsuit it originally filed
 1
     warrants immediate dismissal under Rules 12(b)(1) and 12(h)(3) of the Federal Rules of Civil
 2
     Procedure. Article III standing is a threshold jurisdictional prerequisite central to subject matter
 3
     jurisdiction, and any such defects at the outset of a lawsuit are incurable and warrant dismissal.
 4
     See Bates v. United Parcel Service, Inc., 511 F.3d 974, 985 (9th Cir. 2007) (en banc)
 5
            D.​     Even If the Court Were to Find Standing At Commencement, The Claims
 6                  Jefferies Originally Filed Were No Longer Redressible When They Were
                    Later Assigned to JFUN, Which Destroyed Article III Jurisdiction.
 7
            Even if the Court were to find a basis for standing at commencement (which it should
 8
     not), Jefferies’s opposition makes a clear admission that, after this case was filed, Silo
 9
     assigned-away any rights that Jefferies purported to have at the outset of this case to a Jefferies
10
     subsidiary, which would have impaired the rights that Jefferies claimed to have in such claims
11
     that were already asserted:
12
            [A]fter the original Complaint was filed Silo transferred its remaining interests
13          (not Jefferies’s interests) in the Affected Receivables to Jefferies’s subsidiary,
            JFUN. Then, once Dasagroup’s invoice fraud was uncovered, the interests that
14          Silo had assigned to JFUN were transferred to Jefferies to consolidate all relevant
            interests.
15
16   Opp. at 14:4-7.
            Apart from stating that the assignment to JFUN AR was disclosed in prior filings,
17
     Jeferies does little to explain why that assignment by Silo to a third party (which is referenced as
18
     occurring before the FAC was filed) would not have been fatal to the Article III standing it
19
     vigorously defends. After all, a “Jefferies subsidiary” like JFUN AR is still treated as a legally
20
     distinct and separate entity from Jefferies; otherwise, why would it have filed a UCC amendment
21
     against Dasagroup in Washington state as JFUN AR and not as Jefferies? Jefferies has done
22
     little to illuminate the shell game it is playing in the dark, beyond everyone’s scrutiny (i.e., the
23
     parties, the public, and even this Court), and it has failed to meet its burden in response to
24
     Dasagroup’s jurisdictional challenge.
25          The law is clear that even when a plaintiff can show that it could meet the requirements
26   for standing when a case was initially filed, a plaintiff will lose such standing when it sells its
27   claims or causes of action to a third party. See, e.g., Sanford Inv. Co. v. Ahlstrom Mach.
28

                  REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS FIRST AM. COMPLAINT
                                                       7            Jefferies Funding v. Dasagroup Holdings et al.
                                                                    No. 3:24-cv-05639-TLT
         Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT          Document 143         Filed 09/10/25          Page 8 of 10


     Holdings, Inc.. 198 F.3d 415, 420 (3d Cir. 1999); AtlantiGas Corp. v. Columbia Gas
 1
     Transmission Corp., 210 Fed. App'x 244, 250 (4th Cir. 2006). This is because by selling its
 2
     claim, the plaintiff’s injury can no longer be “redressed by a favorable decision.” See Lujan, 504
 3
     U.S. at 561; see also, Valdin Invs. Corp. v. Oxbridge Capital Mgmt., LLC, 651 F.App'x 5, 7 (2d
 4
     Cir. 2016) (“Valdin's assignment of its rights extinguished its claims against Oxbridge and
 5
     deprived it of any interest in this litigation. Valdin therefore lacks standing.”) (citing Aaron Ferer
 6
     & Sons Ltd. v. Chase Manhattan Bank, Nat'l Ass'n, 731 F.2d 112, 125 (2d Cir. 1984)).
 7
             Because Jefferies’s briefing and averments of a prior assignment in the FAC demonstrate
 8
     that any standing would have been lost by an intervening assignment of rights from Silo to JFUN
 9   AR, the Court should again dismiss this action for Jefferies’s failure to maintain Article III
10   standing on the original complaint it filed during the pendency of this action, before its latest
11   amendment, which cannot resurrect subject matter jurisdiction that has been lost by an
12   intervening assignment
13    II.​   THE THIRD CLAIM IS TIME-BARRED.
14           A.​    The Third Claim Seeks Treble Damages and Is Governed By a One-Year
                    Statute; The Opposition Does Not Dispute This.
15
             Jefferies does not dispute that it makes a claim for treble damages under Cal. Penal Code
16
     section 496 in its First Amended Complaint. See FAC 103. Specifically, FAC 103 states:
17
     “Accordingly, Ward and Dasagroup are liable to Jefferies under Cal. Penal Code § 496(c), and
18
     Jefferies is entitled to three times the amount of Jefferies’s and Silo’s actual damages, costs of
19
     suit, and reasonable attorney’s fees.” This claim for treble damages is the only claim for
20
     damages made in the Third Claim for relief under Penal Code section 496. Such a claim is
21
     punitive in nature, and is thus governed by a one year statute of limitations. See Le v. Prestige
22   Cmty. Credit Union, 2023 U.S.Dist.LEXIS 232717, at *25 (C.D.Cal. Nov. 6, 2023); Prudential
23   Home Mortg. Co., 66 Cal. App. 4th 1242 (1998).
24           The cases cited by Jefferies do not address the punitive nature of the damages under Cal.
25   Penal Code 496. The court in Le v. Prestige Cmty. Credit Union addressed many of those same
26   cases in its opinion and found them unpersuasive. See Le v. Prestige Cmty. Credit Union, 2023
27   U.S.Dist.LEXIS 232717 at *24-25 (collecting and distinguishing several cases finding three

28   years based upon improper presumption that the longer limitations period of C.C.P. § 338

     applied). The Court was clear that this was a faulty analysis, which is the same error made by
 1
     Jefferies here:
 2
 3           A civil claim under California Penal Code § 496(c) may be brought for "three times the
             amount of actual damages," which constitute treble damages. "[T]he settled rule in
 4
             California is that statutes which provide for recovery of damages additional to actual
 5           losses incurred, such as double or treble damages, are considered penal in nature [], and

24   Dkt. 1 (Orig. Compl.). ¶¶ 27, 30, 31, 60. These allegations were the basis of Jefferies’s claims

                                  15          This case has been referred to the undersigned for all discovery purposes. See Dkt. 74.
                                  16   Now pending before the Court is a joint letter brief regarding a dispute between Plaintiff Jefferies
                                  17   Funding (“Jefferies”) and Defendant Dasagroup Holdings (“Dasagroup”) as to whether (a)

                                  22                                          LEGAL STANDARD
                                  23          The relevant legal standards for discovery are well-known and summarized
                                  24   herein. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(b)(1) delineates the scope of discovery in federal civil
                                  25   actions and provides that “[p]arties may obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter that
                                  26   is relevant to any party's claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case.” (emphasis
                                  27   added). Rule 26(b)(5) requires that “[w]hen a party withholds information otherwise discoverable
                                  28   by claiming that the information is privileged or subject to protection as trial-preparation material,
                                         Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 142         Filed 09/10/25     Page 2 of 7




                                   1   the party must: (i) expressly make the claim; and (ii) describe the nature of the documents,

                                   2   communications, or tangible things not produced or disclosed—and do so in a manner that,

                                   3   without revealing information itself privileged or protected, will enable other parties to assess the

                                   4   claim.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5).

                                   5          “The attorney-client privilege protects confidential communications between attorneys and

                                   6   clients, which are made for the purpose of giving legal advice.” In re Grand Jury, 23 F.4th 1088,

                                   7   1091 (9th Cir. 2021) (quoting United States v. Sanmina Corp., 968 F.3d 1107, 1116 (9th Cir.

                                   8   2020)). The privilege attaches when “(1) legal advice of any kind is sought (2) from a

                                   9   professional legal adviser in his capacity as such, (3) the communications relating to that purpose,

                                  10   (4) made in confidence (5) by the client, (6) are at his instance permanently protected (7) from

                                  11   disclosure by himself or by the legal adviser, (8) unless the protection be waived.” United States

                                  12   v. Ruehle, 583 F.3d 600, 607 (9th Cir. 2009) (quoting In re Grand Jury Investigation, 974 F.2d
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   1068, 1071 n.2 (9th Cir. 1992)). The privilege protects only communications and not underlying

                                  14   facts. Upjohn v. United States, 449 U.S. 383, 396 (1981) (holding that a party “may not refuse to

                                  15   disclose any relevant fact within his knowledge merely because he incorporated a statement of

                                  16   such fact into his communication to his attorney”).

                                  17          The attorney-client privilege is “narrowly and strictly construed,” and the party asserting it

                                  18   has the burden of proving that the privilege applies. United States v. Gray, 876 F.2d 1411, 1415

                                  19   (9th Cir. 1989) (citations omitted). The Ninth Circuit has “previously recognized a number of

                                  20   means of sufficiently establishing the privilege, one of which is the privilege log approach.” N re

                                  21   Grand Jury, 974 F.2d at 1071. “The Ninth Circuit has held that a party meets its burden of

                                  22   demonstrating the applicability of the attorney-client privilege by submitting a log that identifies

                                  23   (a) the attorney and client involved, (b) the nature of the document, (c) all persons or entities

                                  24   shown on the document to have received or sent the document, (d) all persons or entities known to

                                  25   have been furnished the document or informed of its substance, and (e) the date the document was

                                  26   generated, prepared, or dated.” Khasin v. Hershey Co., No. 5:12-cv-01862-EJD-PSG, 2014 WL

                                  27   690278, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 21, 2014) (citing In re Grand Jury, 974 F.2d at 1071); see also Club

                                  28   Level, Inc. v. City of Wenatchee, 619 Fed. Appx. 316, 319 (9th Cir. 2015) (affirming district

                                   1   court’s determination that challenged privilege log satisfied Rule 26(b)(5) where privilege log

                                   2   “disclosed the nature of the correspondence, the date of sending, the sender and recipient(s), and a

                                   3   brief statement describing the subject of the content.”).

                                   4          The Court has broad discretion and authority to manage discovery. U.S. Fidelity & Guar.

                                   5   Co. v. Lee Inv. LLC, 641 F.3d 1126, 1136 n.10 (9th Cir. 2011) (“District courts have wide latitude

                                   6   in controlling discovery, and their rulings will not be overturned in the absence of a clear abuse of

                                   7   discretion.”); Laub v. U.S. Dep’t of Int., 342 F.3d 1080, 1093 (9th Cir. 2003). As part of its

                                   8   inherent discretion and authority, the Court has broad discretion in determining relevancy for

                                   9   discovery purposes. Surfvivor Media, Inc. v. Survivor Prods., 406 F.3d 625, 635 (9th Cir. 2005)

                                  10   (citing Hallett v. Morgan, 296 F.3d 732, 751 (9th Cir. 2002)). A court’s determination as to

                                  12   Hospitality Group LLC, 95 F.4th 730, 737–38 (9th Cir. 2024) (finding district court did not abuse
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   discretion on proportionality ruling). Ultimately, “the timing, sequencing and proportionality of

                                  14   discovery is left to the discretion of the Court.” Toro v. Centene Corp., No. 19-cv-05163 LHK

                                  15   (NC), 2020 WL 6108643, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 14, 2020). The Court’s discretion extends to

                                  16   crafting discovery orders that may expand, limit, or differ from the relief requested. See

                                  17   Crawford-El v. Britton, 523 U.S. 574, 598 (1998) (holding trial courts have “broad discretion to

                                  18   tailor discovery narrowly and to dictate the sequence of discovery”). For example, the Court may

                                  19   limit the scope of any discovery method if it determines that “the discovery sought is unreasonably

                                  23   I.     PRIVILEGE LOG DISPUTE

                                  24          Dasagroup’s privilege log at issue includes, for each row corresponding to a withheld

                                  25   email document, the following fields of information: (a) beginning and ending Bates numbers, (b)

                                  26   Custodian, (c) Sent Date and Sent Time, (d) Email From, (e) Email To, (f) Email CC, (g) Email

                                  27   BCC, (h) Email Subject, (i) File Name, (j) File Author, (k) Privilege Claimed, and (l) Privilege

                                  28   Description/General Subject Matter. [Dkt. 125 at 8].
                                                                                         3
                                         Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 142         Filed 09/10/25      Page 4 of 7




                                   1          With regard to certain entries for which Dasagroup redacted the “Email Subject” and “File

                                   2   Name” fields, Jefferies argues that Dasagroup’s privilege log is insufficient to establish the

                                   3   assertion of privilege. Id. at 1-2. Jefferies complains that these redactions fail to provide the

                                   4   necessary information about the subject matter of these withheld documents, so as to allow

                                   5   Jefferies to have a basis to determine whether the assertion of privilege is justified or not.

                                   6          Dasagroup argues that the “Email Subject” lines from the withheld emails are themselves

                                   7   privileged attorney-client communications and that they were redacted in order to avoid disclosing

                                   8   the contents of those attorney-client communications embodied in the Email Subject lines. Id. at

                                   9   3-4. Similarly, Dasagroup argues that the “File Names” of attachments to emails are such that the

                                  10   names disclose attorney-client communications as well, and thus were redacted to avoid disclosing

                                  11   those privileged attorney-client communications inherent in the File Names. Id.

                                  12          To the extent Jefferies seeks an order requiring the privilege log entries to be unredacted or
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   amended to reveal these redacted Email Subject lines and File Names, that remedy is not well-

                                  14   supported by Ninth Circuit law. As discussed above, the Ninth Circuit does not require a privilege

                                  15   log to contain a verbatim recitation of the email subject line of a withheld email. In re Grand

                                  16   Jury, 974 F.2d at 1071. Under Ninth Circuit standards, what is required for a privilege log in this

                                  17   respect is “a brief statement describing the subject of the content” of the document (i.e., the nature

                                  18   of the document). Id.; see also Club Level, 619 Fed. Appx. at 319. To the extent an email subject

                                  19   line or a file name reasonably constitutes an attorney-client communication in and of itself,

                                  20   redacting that information from a privilege log does not run afoul of the Ninth Circuit’s standards

                                  21   or Rule 26(b)(5).

                                  22          However, Jefferies argues that the final column or field for these privilege log entries,

                                  23   titled “Privilege Description/General Subject Matter,” is equally deficient because for these

                                  24   redacted entries Dasagroup has not provided any description of the contents or even general nature

                                  25   of the withheld documents. [Dkt. 125 at 1-2]. Rather, the “Privilege Description/General Subject

                                  28   with nothing more. Id. For example, the entirety of one such challenged entry states in the
